item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports validating diagnostics against seeded faults, but does not establish NextItNet-specific probe reliability. [Mutation-Guided Metamorphic Testing (2024/2025)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/stvr.1898) selects tests by their ability to detect mutated planners; [MDPMorph (2025)](https://valerio-terragni.github.io/assets/pdf/li-ase-2025.pdf) calibrates temporal metamorphic relations and measures mutant detection in reinforcement learning. These provide transferable methods, not recommender evidence. [Time to Split (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16289) shows that sequential-recommender splitting strategies can change rankings and that leave-one-out permits global temporal leakage; this motivates documenting the supplied protocol’s limitations while preserving the host’s fixed splits.\n\nAttribution sensitivity alone is insufficient evidence of diagnostic usefulness. [A Fresh Look at Sanity Checks (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.02383) identifies noise and similarity-measure problems in parameter-randomization tests, proposing Smooth and Efficient MPRT. Suggested NextItNet adaptation: bounded mutants for count-minus-one readout, nonzero padding propagation, noncausal convolution, and shifted-target exposure; verify earlier features remain invariant to future-token changes, and final readout selects the last nonpadding position. Use unmodified implementations and semantics-preserving transformations as negative controls; estimate per-fault sensitivity and clean-control specificity with uncertainty, separating threshold calibration from assessment. These are proposed tests, not published NextItNet findings. Establish incremental value beyond margins and candidate ranks through prespecified diagnostic ablations and prospective single-model interventions, judged solely by unchanged host macro validation HR@10. Keep one trained checkpoint per category; diagnostic success does not itself establish recommendation improvement."}
